title: Staying on one chord: banjo style demanded by the trumpet players
summary: Old trumpet players wanted banjo to hold one position per chord, with only the bass moving.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And how did you play, I guess you played banjo with them. How did you play your banjo with them? Is there any different to the way you play with these bands now?

Well, I mean, during that time those musicians didn't want you. In other words, if you had 12 beats to make on A flat, you just make it right there. Don't move your fingers off it. That's where those musicians want you to play then. No, they don't tell you you play like you want. You want to make A flat here, A flat up here, you know, break it there.
just keep it. Stay right there.
Yeah, one card. That card change, change, and one, stay right there. That's where it...
Right back there up in the end of the neck.
now you mean you go all over?

Yeah, you can go all over because I don't say anything now. But during them days, that's it, those trumpet players, they wouldn't hire. You wouldn't do it, they weren't hire anymore. See what I'm saying?
They just wanted the straight, solid chorus.
That's it, all the way through. No moving up.
Do you think that made for a better sound in the band?

Well, I guess... A better rhythm or would it be any easier to... I guess it would make the sound more solid, you know. I think it would, you know, because they didn't have anything with a bass violin behind. It was bass violin and the band was only instrument with some kind of volume, drum, there's nothing of that, but that's what they want, you know. The only man would move up and down would be the bass, you see. Still, if you had 12 beats on A flat, you just hold that A flat and the bass, he runs his A flat like he want.
